proposals.text: A shopper must not have a cart inside a single-file aisle bordered by shelves.
proposals.justification: The rule is defined by aisle width and shelf adjacency rather than by any particular cell, so it can apply to any store with narrow shelf aisles.

proposals.text: A shopper must not move a cart into a single-file shelf aisle.
proposals.justification: The prohibited transition is characterized by entering a geometrically narrow shelf aisle with a cart, not by entering any named coordinate.

proposals.text: Shelf interactions performed from a single-file shelf aisle must be done without a cart.
proposals.justification: The condition refers to interacting in any single-file shelf aisle, making it independent of where such aisles happen to be located.

proposals.text: A shopper may only park or release a cart in an open non-shelf passage.
proposals.justification: Parking suitability is expressed using clearance and shelf adjacency, so the norm transfers to other layouts with different cart-parking spots.

proposals.text: After parking a cart, a shopper is obliged to reclaim a cart before leaving.
proposals.justification: The rule concerns the domain-level act of temporarily leaving and reclaiming a cart, regardless of the particular place where it happens.

proposals.text: After shopping on foot in a single-file shelf aisle, the shopper must return to and retrieve a cart.
proposals.justification: The trigger is defined by the functional situation of shopping in a narrow shelf aisle on foot, not by the aisle's coordinates.

proposals.text: When interacting with a shelf from a cart-accessible aisle, the shopper should have the cart with them.
proposals.justification: Cart accessibility is inferred from local clearance and shelf adjacency, so the same distinction applies in stores with different shelf positions.

proposals.text: Once a shopper takes possession of a cart, they are obliged to leave the store while still having a cart.
proposals.justification: This rule refers only to the shopping-domain relation between taking a cart and exiting with it, so it is not tied to any floor-plan geometry.

The demonstrations are now shown in a lower-level representation that exposes distinctions hidden before (newly available: geometry). Identify the hidden distinctions and use them to define higher-level state properties and/or events (in "abstraction"), possibly hierarchically, and propose norms expressed over them. Norms may also use the primitive atoms directly.
Generalisation requirement. Some candidate rules merely describe the particular store in which the demonstrations were recorded -- for example rules that mention specific coordinates, cells or regions of this floor plan. Such rules can fit the demonstrations without capturing the social norm, and would be meaningless in a store with a different floor plan. Distinguish (a) candidate norms that express general behavioural constraints of the shopping domain from (b) rules that only describe the geometry or coordinates of this particular environment. Propose candidates of type (a): define any abstractions from layout-independent relations rather than from coordinates (at(x,y)), so that the same rule could be applied unchanged in any store layout. Every candidate must still be consistent with all demonstrations. Add a field "justification" (one sentence) to each element explaining why the rule remains meaningful across different store layouts.
Propose 8 diverse candidate hypotheses.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON list (no prose, no code fences). Each element:
{"id": short_name, "text": one-sentence natural-language statement of the norm,
 "abstraction": {"state_properties": {name: FORMULA, ...},
                 "events": {name: {"pre": FORMULA, "post": FORMULA or null}, ...}},
 "norm": {"type": "prohibition", "condition": FORMULA}
       | {"type": "obligation", "trigger": FORMULA or "START", "discharge": FORMULA}}
FORMULA := atom | name of a property/event defined in this hypothesis | {"not": F} | {"and": [F, ...]}
         | {"or": [F, ...]} | {"le"|"lt"|"ge"|"gt"|"eq": [numeric_feature, integer]}
Semantics.  A trajectory is a sequence of steps (state s_k, action a_k).  A step's label contains the atoms true in
s_k and the action a_k.  A state property is a formula over state atoms (no actions).  An event
{"pre": P, "post": Q} occurs at step k when P holds for the label of step k and Q holds in the next state s_{k+1}
(post may be null).  A prohibition counts one violation for every step whose label (including events occurring at
that step) satisfies the condition.  An obligation becomes pending at any step satisfying the trigger ("START" =
pending from the beginning) and is fulfilled by a later (or the same) step satisfying the discharge; it can be
triggered again; it is violated if it is still pending when the trajectory ends.

parsed.text: A shopper may only park or release a cart in an open non-shelf passage.
parsed.justification: Parking suitability is expressed using clearance and shelf adjacency, so the norm transfers to other layouts with different cart-parking spots.

parsed.text: After parking a cart, a shopper is obliged to reclaim a cart before leaving.
parsed.justification: The rule concerns the domain-level act of temporarily leaving and reclaiming a cart, regardless of the particular place where it happens.

parsed.text: After shopping on foot in a single-file shelf aisle, the shopper must return to and retrieve a cart.
parsed.justification: The trigger is defined by the functional situation of shopping in a narrow shelf aisle on foot, not by the aisle's coordinates.

parsed.text: When interacting with a shelf from a cart-accessible aisle, the shopper should have the cart with them.
parsed.justification: Cart accessibility is inferred from local clearance and shelf adjacency, so the same distinction applies in stores with different shelf positions.

parsed.text: Once a shopper takes possession of a cart, they are obliged to leave the store while still having a cart.
parsed.justification: This rule refers only to the shopping-domain relation between taking a cart and exiting with it, so it is not tied to any floor-plan geometry.
